articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These actions target entities deemed to be involved in the theft or misappropriation of U.S. intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. The specifics of the licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences while maintaining the pressure on illicit activities.

The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American innovation and technology from foreign adversaries and illicit actors. Further details on the designated entities and the scope of the General Licenses are available on the Treasury website.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License, modifying previous authorizations concerning transactions involving the country. This amendment aims to refine the scope of permissible activities under the existing sanctions regime.

Accompanying the amended General License, OFAC also published a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to provide clarity and guidance to stakeholders regarding the updated provisions. The FAQ addresses common inquiries and helps ensure compliance with the evolving sanctions landscape.

These adjustments reflect the U.S. government's ongoing evaluation of its sanctions policies towards Venezuela, seeking to balance humanitarian considerations with the broader foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to Iran and Cuba. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued new and amended General Licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions. These measures aim to provide clarity on permissible transactions and to mitigate any unintended impacts of the new sanctions.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on both Iran and Cuba, addressing concerns related to human rights, proliferation, and support for terrorism.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Removal of Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a recalibration of sanctions measures concerning certain individuals or entities previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals typically follow a review process and may be influenced by changes in behavior, policy shifts, or other relevant factors. The specific reasons for this removal were not immediately detailed.
This development signals a potential, albeit limited, easing of pressure on certain actors within the Venezuelan context, while the broader sanctions framework remains in place.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and international stability.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating the flow of illegal drugs and preventing the financing of terrorist organizations globally. The specific targets were not immediately detailed in the announcement.

These measures are part of a broader strategy to isolate and financially cripple those who engage in or facilitate narcotics trafficking and terrorist acts, thereby protecting the U.S. financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, International Criminal Court Designation, and Burma-Related Designation Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, resolving apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally.

In separate actions, OFAC also issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated General Licenses, indicating a targeted response to specific activities. Additionally, a Burma-related designation was removed, signaling a potential shift in policy or a change in circumstances for the delisted entity.

These diverse actions demonstrate OFAC's multifaceted approach to sanctions enforcement, encompassing civil penalties, new designations, and strategic removals based on evolving geopolitical considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License. This license authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the existing Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are often issued to clarify the scope of sanctions, facilitate humanitarian aid, or allow for specific types of commercial activities that are deemed not to undermine the overall policy objectives of the sanctions.

The specifics of this new General License will be crucial for entities engaged in activities related to Russia, providing clarity on permissible conduct and reducing the risk of inadvertent sanctions violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities and individuals connected to Iran. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to counter Iran's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued a new Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions. Additionally, an existing Russia-related General License was amended, further refining the scope of permissible activities under the Russia sanctions program.
These measures reflect the U.S. government's dynamic approach to sanctions, adapting to evolving threats and ensuring that humanitarian and other legitimate activities can continue where appropriate.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals, Updates, and Publication of Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designation removals and updates, indicating a recalibration of its sanctions lists. These changes often reflect new information, changes in circumstances, or successful remediation efforts by previously designated parties.

In addition to the list adjustments, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert, providing guidance and warnings regarding specific risks or illicit activities associated with Iran. This alert aims to help financial institutions and businesses identify and mitigate potential exposure.

Furthermore, an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) was released, offering updated clarity on existing regulations and compliance expectations for transactions involving Iran. These publications collectively aim to enhance transparency and facilitate compliance within the complex sanctions environment.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This OFAC action is part of a broader set of enforcement actions by the U.S. Treasury Department against Bank of America, which also includes significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures.

The settlement underscores the critical importance for financial institutions to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent illicit transactions and adhere to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), incurring a civil penalty of $175,015. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The enforcement action highlights the responsibility of logistics and shipping companies to ensure their operations do not facilitate transactions with sanctioned entities or in sanctioned jurisdictions. Compliance failures in this sector can lead to significant financial penalties.
This case serves as a reminder for companies involved in international trade and logistics to implement comprehensive sanctions compliance programs to mitigate risks and avoid penalties.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a historic $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread deficiencies and ineffectiveness in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould stated that despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML program, the bank's compliance continues to show breakdowns in internal controls, posing a threat to U.S. national and economic security.

The OCC found that the bank's deficient transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to a large number of late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah (bank), for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has assessed a substantial $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for its failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks.

FinCEN found that Bank of America willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate anti-money laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

The penalty addresses the bank's failure to timely report over $5 billion in suspicious activity between 2018 and 2025, including activities related to Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border. This action represents the third-largest penalty in Treasury history.

articles.headline: BIS Issues Guidance Defining 'U.S. Content' for USMCA Metals-Derivative Equipment
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published new guidance on October 14, 2026, defining 'U.S. content' under Proclamation 11032 for USMCA metals-derivative equipment. This definition includes U.S. parts and, where not otherwise accounted for, U.S.-melted-and-poured steel, U.S.-smelted-and-cast aluminum, and U.S.-smelted-and-cast copper.

Under the new U.S. Note 16(j), heading 9903.82.20 imposes a 25% duty on non-U.S. content and on U.S. content exceeding 40% of an article's value. This guidance is crucial for manufacturers and exporters operating under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
The clarification aims to provide greater certainty for businesses in determining the origin and content of their products, impacting tariff assessments and compliance with trade regulations.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
